newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Four centuries on, Cossacks retreat from Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Four centuries on, Cossacks retreat from Chechnya.

text.p: Vasily Kutko, Cossack Ataman of this tiny, mud-strewn village, stared out sadly over the snow-covered expanse of the Chechen steppe.
"My grandfathers and their grandfathers helped settle this land. Their graves are all here. But soon I fear there will be no trace left of us," he said, face contorting into an icy wind.
Centuries after they helped tame the Caucasus region for the tsars, Russian Cossacks are leaving in droves, fearing there is no place for them in the de facto independent Moslem republic.
Yet some Cossack leaders in Russia vow revenge for Russia's military defeat in Chechnya, and many people believe Cossack-Chechen relations are potentially explosive.
SPECIAL ROLE IN RUSSIAN HISTORY
For four centuries until the 1917 Bolshevik revolution, Russia relied on free Cossack soldiers to defend and expand the southern frontiers of its empire.
Ethnic Slavs, they carved out a culture based on fiercely free-spirited warrior traditions and stood out for their flamboyant battle garb and love of song and drink.
The tsars rewarded them with tracts of land, keeping them broadly free of the feudal shackles which bound most impoverished Russian peasants.

In Russia's drive southward they met fierce resistance from groups like the Chechens, who inhabited the snow-capped Caucasus mountains between what was then Russia and its Turkish or Persian enemies. Tens of thousands settled in what is now the north of present-day Chechnya.
But millions died during Soviet dictator Josef Stalin's forced collectivisation of the 1920s and 1930s. Their identity nearly died out before political reforms of the 1980s.
REFORMS BROUGHT COSSACK REBIRTH, BUT ALSO TENSION
"After 1985 we started organising, trying to revive our traditions," said Kutko, 62, chosen Ataman, or leader of the Cossack minority in this tiny village three years ago.
But the period also saw a rise in Chechen nationalism including the election of separatist President Dzhokhar Dudayev in 1991, and trouble brewed between Cossacks and Chechens.
Russia's bloody attempt to crush the rebel republic's independence drive aggravated matters. Cossacks were seen by many Chechens as supporting Moscow's troops.

Another source of tension was a call by some Cossacks that northern Chechnya, where they have traditionally lived, be transferred to the control of an adjacent Russian region, though most of their leaders admit this is unrealistic.

"The Chechens say this will be an Islamic republic. What about the rest of us who aren't Moslems?" asked Kutko. "I've had grenades and Molotov cocktails tossed into my yard. I've had letters saying: 'Russian pigs out of Chechnya!'"
Kutko said violent incidents by Chechens against Cossacks went uninvestigated. The Chechen authorities say they are doing their best to protect their rights with limited resources.
"When night begins, fear begins," said his plump sister Klavdiya, 71, dressed in a scarlet robe. "Every time the cat makes a noise I think it means the end."
COSSACKS VOTE WITH THEIR FEET, AND FOR MASKHADOV
Many Cossack families have already left and "For sale" signs are planted in front of many single-storey wooden houses.

Sergei Dontsov, an adviser on Cossack issues to the Russian government, said only 10 percent of an original 30,000 Cossack families remain in the republic. Financial problems prevent more from leaving. Kutko's spartan house is worth only $3,000 in Chechnya, while a replacement would cost $20,000 in Russia.
Kutko and other Cossacks voted overwhelmingly for Aslan Maskhadov, the moderate Chechen guerrilla commander who won the region's presidency last month.
He said he hoped Maskhadov could ease tensions, even if it meant an independent Chechen state.

"We are pinning all of our hopes on him. We think that our new president can put an end to this chaos," he said. "After all, we lived in peace side by side with Chechens for decades and we have a great deal in common," says Klavdiya.
But other Cossack leaders, lamenting Russia's battlefield humiliation at the hands of tiny Chechnya, say they are gearing up for a new war, vowing not to tolerate Chechen independence.
Vladimir Ponamaryov, a Cossack Ataman in southern Russia, growled angrily when asked about Chechens.

"Grozny (the regional Chechen capital) has never been Chechen, and it won't be. We saved them from the Turks, who would have slaughtered them all if it weren't for Christian Russia. Chechens have always just been bandits," he said.
"If we had been called on to do the job then we would have annihilated them all, left nothing behind but ashes," he says of the war. "Next time the Chechens won't be so lucky."
Ponamaryov, who heads the Pyatigorsk section of the Ter Cossacks, says his forces have arms and that they want more.
"We have weapons and we have people who can fight in the best Cossack traditions. If those Chechen bandits can have grenades and rockets, why can't we defend ourselves?"
Dontsov said some four million people in Russia claimed Cossack ancestry, but only a fraction were active in military formations.
Some, especially the more radical Ter Cossacks, want to police the de facto border between Chechnya and Russia itself.
"Right now there is 700 km (400 miles) of unguarded frontier between us and Chechnya. But at this stage it is not serious to talk about Cossacks policing it adequately," said Dontsov.
Some observers dismissed the fiery rhetoric of Atamans like Ponomaryov, saying the Cossacks possess neither the will nor the power to fight Chechens.
But Dontsov said Chechen-Cossack disputes were a powderkeg. "One spark could set off terrible bloodshed," he says.
